Canada's tax system contains a few reporting regimes. At high-level, there is a requirement to report (1) "reportable transactions"; (2) "notifiable transactions"; and (3) "uncertain tax treatments". 
(1) Reportable Transactions
A transaction is a reportable transaction if: (i) it is a transaction or series of transactions that has at least one of the three generic hallmarks; and (ii) it can reasonably be concluded that one of the main purposes of entering into the transaction or series of transactions is to obtain a tax benefit. 

(2) Notifiable Transactions
Notifiable transactions include both transactions that the Canadian tax atuhority has found to be abusive and transactions identified as transactions of interest. The Minister of National Revenue has the authority to designate, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance, transactions or series of transactions for purposes of the notifiable transaction rules. 

(3) Reportable Uncertain Tax Treatments
 An uncertain tax treatment is a tax treatment used, or planned to be used, in an entity's income tax filings for which there is uncertainty over whether the tax treatment will be accepted as being in accordance with tax law.

Apart from hallmarks introduced by MDR standard (focused on CRS avoidance), DAC6 sets out more detailed hallmark categories covering wider area of risk prone cross-border arrangements. There are five categories of such hallmarks: (A) generic, (B) specific, (C) cross-border tax hallmarks, (D) CRS avoidance & opaque structures, (E) transfer pricing. Some of these hallmarks are subject to a “main benefit test,” while others apply regardless of tax advantage.

Key items of information to be disclosed:
i)	Identification of parties - names, dates and places of birth (for individuals), tax residence(s), Tax Identification Numbers (TINs), persons or entities considered intermediaries and their details, persons or entities considered relevant taxpayers and their details, associated enterprises of the taxpayer(s) where relevant.
ii)	Details of the hallmarks - which specific hallmark(s) (from Categories A–E) make the arrangement reportable, whether the main benefit test is satisfied (if applicable).
iii)	Summary of the arrangement - a concise description of the arrangement, including its name if commonly known (however the summary must not disclose commercial, industrial, or professional secrets, or information contrary to public policy).
iv)	Date of first step - when the first step in implementing the arrangement was or will be carried out.
v)	Details of domestic provisions - the national legal provisions forming the basis of the arrangement (e.g., specific articles of Czech or other EU tax law relied upon).
vi)	Value of the arrangement - the value of the cross-border arrangement (usually expressed as the amount involved, expected tax advantage, or transaction value).
vii)	Affected Member States - identification of the EU Member State(s) of the relevant taxpayer(s), any other Member States that are likely to be affected.
viii)	Other affected jurisdictions - identification of any other person in an EU Member State who is likely to be affected by the arrangement.

In the case of the so called “marketable arrangement” (i.e. standardized cross-border arrangement that is designed, marketed, ready for implementation or made available for implementation without a need to be substantially customized) there is also a specific requirement to submit regular notifications of changes to such standardized cross-border arrangement which was already reported.

Under DAC6 not every cross-border tax arrangement must be reported. Several conditions must be met before the disclosure obligation arises.
1. Cross-border element
The arrangement must be cross-border. That means it concerns either: 
i)	more than one EU Member State; or
ii)	EU Member State and a third country.
Typical indicators of cross-border relevance include:
i)	the participants are tax resident in different jurisdictions;
ii)	an entity is resident in two or more jurisdictions;
iii)	business is carried out in another jurisdiction via a permanent establishment; or
iv)	activities have an impact on the automatic exchange of information (specifically CRS reporting).
Purely domestic arrangements are outside DAC6.
2. Presence of a hallmark
The arrangement must contain at least one hallmark defined in Annex IV of DAC6.
Category A – Generic hallmarks (e.g. confidentiality clauses, success fee linked to tax advantage).
Category B – Specific hallmarks (e.g. loss-buying, income conversion, circular transactions).
Category C – Cross-border hallmarks (e.g. double deductions, double relief, tax-exempt income, mismatches in valuation).
Category D – CRS avoidance & opaque ownership (e.g. non-transparent structures designed to hide beneficial owners or circumvent CRS reporting).
Category E – Transfer pricing (e.g. use of unilateral safe harbours, hard-to-value intangibles, transfers eroding earnings).
3. Main Benefit Test (MBT) – where applicable
Some hallmarks (mainly categories A, B, and some C) only trigger reporting if the main benefit test is satisfied.
The MBT asks whether, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, the main benefit or one of the main benefits that a person may reasonably expect from the arrangement is the obtaining of a tax advantage.
If no tax advantage is a main benefit, then those hallmarks do not apply.
Other hallmarks (such as certain mismatches, CRS avoidance, or transfer pricing arrangements) apply without the MBT.
4. Timeline condition
The arrangement must be reportable within 30 days of:
i)	being made available for implementation; 
ii)	being ready for implementation; or
iii)	when the first step in implementation has been made.
Retroactive reporting also applied for arrangements implemented between 25 June 2018 and 30 June 2020 (the “look-back period”).
5. EU nexus of the reporter
The reporting party (intermediary or taxpayer) must have a sufficient link to the EU:
i)	tax residence in an EU Member State;
ii)	a permanent establishment in an EU Member State; 
iii)	incorporation in, or subject to, the laws of an EU Member State; or
iv)	registration with an EU professional association.

In the Czech Republic – as a EU Member State – the MDR standard was implemented under the EU’s binding DAC6 (Directive 2018/822/EU). In case the reference to DAC6 directive is made in the following answers such reference relates also to the Czech Republic MDR implementation without any distinction. 
The main difference between the OECD MDR standard and its EU DAC6 counterpart is that DAC6 regulation focuses specifically on cross-border arrangements that involve at least one EU Member State. Therefore, the applicability of MDR is limited only to arrangements which are related only to the EU internal market. Furthermore, DAC6 mandates automatic exchange of all reported arrangements between EU Member States, ensuring that information circulates across the Union.

Est considéré comme transfrontière tout dispositif prenant la forme d’un accord, d’un montage ou d’un plan ayant ou non force exécutoire et concernant la France et un autre État, membre ou non de l’Union européenne, dès lors que l’une au moins des conditions suivantes est satisfaite :
a) Au moins un des participants au dispositif n'est pas fiscalement domicilié ou résident en France ou n'y a pas son siège ;
b) Au moins un des participants au dispositif est fiscalement domicilié, résident ou a son siège dans plusieurs Etats ou territoires simultanément ;
c) Au moins un des participants au dispositif exerce une activité dans un autre Etat ou territoire par l'intermédiaire d'un établissement stable situé dans cet Etat ou territoire, le dispositif constituant une partie ou la totalité de l'activité de cet établissement stable ;
d) Au moins un des participants au dispositif exerce une activité dans un autre Etat ou territoire sans y être fiscalement domicilié ou résident ni disposer d'établissement stable dans cet Etat ou territoire ;
e) Le dispositif peut avoir des conséquences sur l'échange automatique d'informations entre Etats ou territoires ou sur l'identification des bénéficiaires effectif

Les conditions pour qu’un dispositif transfrontière soit visé par l'obligation de déclaration sont les suivantes :

Un dispositif transfrontière doit être déclaré lorsqu’il comporte un ou plusieurs marqueurs. Un marqueur est une caractéristique ou particularité d'un dispositif transfrontière, qui indique un risque d'évasion fiscale correspondant à l’un de ceux recensés à l'annexe IV de la directive (UE) 2018/822 du Conseil du 25 mai 2018 qui a été transposée l’article 1649 AH du CGI.

Les quinze marqueurs DAC 6 sont regroupés en cinq catégories selon le risque potentiel d’évasion fiscale qu’ils entendent couvrir :
- Marqueur A : marqueurs généraux liés au critère de l’avantage principal (A1 : dispositif soumis à une clause de confidentialité ; A2 : dispositif pour lequel la rémunération des intermédiaires est liée à l’avantage fiscal obtenu ; A3 : dispositifs commercialisables)
- Marqueur B : marqueurs généraux liés au critère de l’avantage principal (B1 : acquisition d’une société avec des pertes pour utilisation de ces dernières à des fins fiscales. B2 : conversion de revenus en capital/dons/recettes taxables à un niveau inférieur. B3 : transactions circulaires.)
- Marqueur C : marqueurs spécifiques liés aux opérations transfrontières (C1 : dispositif prévoyant la déduction de paiements transfrontières effectués entre deux ou
plusieurs entreprises associées lorsque : bi : la juridiction du bénéficiaire ne lève pas l’impôt sur les sociétés ou l’applique à un taux zéro ou presque nul. c : le paiement ouvre droit à une exonération. d : le paiement ouvre droit à un régime fiscal préférentiel ; C2 : dispositif prévoyant la double déduction d’un amortissement pour un même actif.
C3 : dispositif prévoyant l’allègement de la double imposition pour le même élément de
revenu ou de capital dans la même juridiction.
C4 : transfert d’actifs dont le traitement fiscal diffère dans une large mesure)
- Marqueur D : marqueurs spécifiques concernant l’échange automatique d’informations et les bénéficiaires effectifs (D1 : dispositif portant atteinte à l’obligation de déclaration découlant de la législation européenne relative aux comptes financiers (DAC2/NCD).
D2 : dispositif faisant intervenir une chaîne de propriété formelle ou effective non
transparente permettant de dissimuler le bénéficiaire effectif)
- Marqueur E : marqueurs spécifiques concernant les prix de transfert (E1 : utilisation de régimes de protection unilatéraux. E2 : transfert d’actifs ou d’incorporels ou de droits portant sur ces actifs, difficiles à évaluer au moment de leur transfert entre entreprises associées. E3 : transfert transfrontière de fonctions et/ou de risques et/ou d’actifs au sein du groupe, si le bénéfice annuel avant intérêts et impôts que le(s) cédant(s) prévoi(en)t de réaliser dans les 3 ans suivant le transfert est inférieur à 50 % du bénéfice annuel avant intérêts et impôts que les mêmes personnes prévoiraient de réaliser si le transfert n’avait pas lieu)

En outre, certaines catégories de marqueur sont considérées comme doubles, et sont soumis au critère de l’avantage principal : marqueurs A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, B3, C1 b) i), C1 c) et C1 d). Cela signifie qu’un dispositif qui révélerait d’un marqueur double ne sera pas systématiquement déclarable. En effet, un tel dispositif ne sera déclarable que s’il génère un avantage fiscal principal au bénéficiaire après une mise en balance des avantages de toute nature générés par le dispositif.

Les dispositifs relevant des marqueurs considérés comme simples sont déclarables sans apprécier si le dispositif procure un avantage fiscal principal au bénéficiaire : marqueurs C1 a), C1 b) ii), C2, C3, C4, D1, D2, E1, E2, E3.

Les obligations sont remplies en premier lieu par les intermédiaires concepteurs de ces dispositifs. A défaut d’intermédiaire ou si cet intermédiaire est soumis au secret professionnel, c’est le contribuable concerné (bénéficiaire du dispositif) qui doit déclarer le dispositif si celui-ci ne donne pas son accord à l’intermédiaire de déclarer les informations exigées.

La directive raisonne donc autour de deux types de déclarants que sont les intermédiaires et les contribuables concernés. Chacun d’entre eux peut être soit un professionnel soit un particulier. In principle, cross-border tax arrangements that meet one of the hallmarks listed in the annex to the DAC6 Directive are reported. In Germany, standardized arrangements (Hallmark A3) are reported most frequently.

The reporting obligation applies to tax arrangements that are subject to the EU Administrative Assistance Act, affect multiple EU member states or one EU member state and one or more third countries (cross-border relevance), and meet at least one hallmark (see Annex to the DAC6 Directive) and, for certain hallmarks, additionally the main benefit test.

In the EU, BEPS Action 12 was adressed by amending the EU Directive on Administrative Cooperation 2011/16/EU through the so-called DAC6 Directive ((EU) 2018/822). This was implemented in Germany by law on December 21, 2019, with effect from January 1, 2020 (see §§ 138d – 138k of the german fiscal code). This introduced an obligation to report cross-border tax arrangements and an automatic exchange of information between EU member states regarding these arrangements.

The obligation to report cross-border tax arrangements affects intermediaries (persons who market such arrangements, design them for third parties, organize them, make them available for use, or manage the implementation by third parties). These are mostly tax and financial advisors. In some cases, however, the user of a tax arrangement is also obliged to report it.

The report must include personal details (name, date of birth if applicable, address, tax identification number, and country of residence) of the reporting intermediary, the user, and any affiliated companies of the user involved in the arrangement. It must specify which hallmark the arrangement falls under and which legal regulations are relevant. Additionally, a summary of the content of the cross-border tax arrangement, including the date of (expected) implementation and the actual or expected economic value of the arrangement, must be provided. Finally, the report should also include the affected EU member states, as well as information on individuals residing in EU member states who are likely to be directly affected by the cross-border tax arrangement.

a) Intermediaries, i.e. any person that designs, markets, organises or makes available for implementation or manages the implementation of a reportable cross-border arrangement. It also means any person that, having regard to the relevant facts and circumstances and based on available information and the relevant expertise and understanding required to provide such services, knows or could be reasonably expected to know that they have undertaken to provide, directly or by means of other persons, aid, assistance or advice with respect to designing, marketing, organising, making available for implementation or managing the implementation of a reportable cross-border arrangement.  

b) Relevant taxpayer, i.e. any person to whom a reportable cross-border arrangement is made available for implementation, or who is ready to implement a reportable cross-border arrangement or has implemented the first step of such an arrangement.

Therefore, cross-border arrangements that contain Hallmark D "Specific hallmarks concerning automatic exchange of information and beneficial ownership" are also reportable.

The specified descriptions for the domestic regime are:
•	The promoter or participant wishes to keep the transaction confidential from Revenue or other promoters,
•	A premium fee attributable to or contingent on the tax advantage might be expected in respect of the transaction,
•	Use of a standardised tax product,
•	A loss scheme for individuals or companies,
•	An employment income scheme,
•	An “income into capital” scheme,
•	The conversion of income into a gift, or
•	A party to the transaction is the trustee of a discretionary trust.
The other conditions which apply to disclosable transactions under the domestic regime are that they enable or might enable a tax advantage, and that obtaining the tax advantage is the main benefit or one of the main benefits that might be expected from the transaction.

For the cross-border regime, a cross-border arrangement is one which involves participants who are not all tax resident in the same jurisdiction, are tax resident in multiple jurisdictions, have a permanent establishment in another jurisdiction, or otherwise operate in another jurisdiction with creating a permanent establishment or being tax resident. A cross-border arrangement also includes arrangements that impact in automatic exchange of information (this includes CRS reporting) and identification of beneficial ownership.
The hallmarks are set out in detail in Annex IV of the Directive. Certain hallmarks also require a main benefit test to be satisfied – that it can be reasonably expected that a tax advantage was the main benefit or one of the main benefits of the transaction.  The hallmarks can be broadly categorised as follows:
•	Generic hallmarks linked to the main benefit test; 
•	Specific hallmarks linked to the main benefit test; 
•	Specific hallmarks related to cross-border transactions (some of which are linked to the main benefit test); 
•	Specific hallmarks concerning automatic exchange of information and beneficial ownership (including CRS avoidance); and 
•	Specific hallmarks concerning transfer pricing.

Under the domestic regime, the initial reporting obligation falls on the promoter of the arrangements. If there is no promoter, or if the promoter claims legal and professional privilege, then the reporting obligation falls to the participant in the arrangements. In certain circumstances, the marketer of the arrangement may also have a requirement to disclose.
Under the cross-border regime, the initial reporting obligation falls on the intermediary. If there is no intermediary, or if they claim legal and professional privilege, then the reporting obligation falls to the participant in the arrangements.
The domestic regime was introduced in 2010. The cross-border regime was introduced in 2019.

Ireland has two sets of mandatory disclosure rules – the domestic Mandatory Disclosure rules for aggressive tax planning (the domestic regime) and the cross-border rules introduced by EU Directive 2018/822 regarding mandatory exchange of information regarding certain reportable cross border arrangements (the cross-border regime).
The domestic regime requires a promoter of disclosable transactions to provide specified information to Revenue within 5 days of the earlier of the first marketing contact, the date the scheme is made available for implementation, or the date the promoter is first aware that any part of the disclosable transaction has been implemented. A promoter is anyone who designs, markets or organises or manages a disclosable transaction, or is otherwise responsible for the organisation or management of that transaction.  If there is no promoter, if the promoter is outside the State, or if the promoter claims legal and professional privilege then the reporting obligation shifts to the person who participates in the disclosable transaction.
The cross-border regime requires an intermediary to a reportable cross border arrangement to provide specified information to Revenue within 30 days beginning on the earlier of the day after the reportable cross border arrangement is made available for implementation, the day after the reportable cross border arrangement is ready for implementation, or when the first implementation step is taken. An intermediary is an individual or entity who designs, markets organises or manages, or makes available a reportable cross border arrangement. They must be resident or have a permanent establishment in a Member State, be incorporated or governed by the laws of a Member State, or be registered with a legal, tax or consultancy professional body in a Member State. If there is no intermediary, or if the intermediary claims legal and professional privilege then the reporting obligation shifts to the person who participates in the reportable cross border arrangement or to whom the reportable cross border arrangement is made available. Avoidance of CRS reporting falls under the cross-border regime.
Under both regimes, a transaction or arrangement that is reported to Revenue is given a unique reference number which must be included on the tax return of the person who entered into the transaction (cross-border regime only) or the person who obtains the tax advantage.
Revenue can impose penalties on those who fail to comply with their obligations under either regime.

Under the domestic regime, the promoter must disclose the basis on which the transaction is considered disclosable, a summary of the transaction and full details of the structure of the transaction, including how the tax advantage arises and details of the relevant tax provisions. They must also provide the details of each person to whom the arrangements have been made available for implementation. 
Where there is no promoter or when legal and professional privilege has been claimed, the person entering the transaction must provide a summary of the transaction and full details of the structure of the transaction, including how the tax advantage arises and details of the relevant tax provisions. They must also provide the name and contact details of the promoter, or their own information if there is no promoter.

Under Section 131E of the Israeli Income Tax Ordinance, taxpayers are required to disclose in their annual tax return any “reportable position.” A reportable position is one where the taxpayer’s chosen interpretation of the law provides a tax advantage, while the Israeli Tax Authority has published a contrary position. The regime is intended to increase transparency and reduce aggressive tax planning by obligating taxpayers to notify the Authority when they rely on an interpretation that differs from its published guidance. Failure to disclose a reportable position may expose the taxpayer to penalties and extended assessment periods.

Similar disclosure provisions exist under Israel’s VAT legislation and customs laws.

In 2023, an amendment was introduced to the CRS Regulations through Regulation 10(j), granting the Director of the Israel Tax Authority the authority to notify a financial institution that an arrangement or transaction is intended to avoid CRS reporting and should therefore be disregarded. 
This mechanism differs from the general MDR regime, as it does not impose a reporting obligation, but it nonetheless serves as a tool to prevent aggressive tax planning in the CRS context.

An arrangement is reportable if it constitutes a “reportable position,” meaning a position that (1) contradicts a position published by the Israel Tax Authority by the end of the relevant tax year, and (2) provides a tax benefit exceeding NIS 5 million in that year or NIS 10 million over four years. A “tax benefit” includes a tax reduction or relief, deferral of a taxable event or payment, avoidance of tax or withholding, or the use of losses or expenses.
In the annual tax return, the taxpayer must disclose that a reportable position has been taken and indicate which specific position was adopted.

Any position that creates a “tax benefit” as defined in the law, is reportable. Each year, the Israel Tax Authority publishes a list of "reportable positions" that meet the statutory conditions. In general, a tax benefit means a reduction of tax, a deferral of tax, or an avoidance of withholding tax.

Some examples of reportable schemes are those that:

1. Involve a foreign resident applying a double taxation agreement signed by Mexico with respect to income not taxed in the taxpayer's country or jurisdiction of tax residence.

2. Involve the transfer of intangible assets that are difficult to value.

3. Involve corporate restructurings in which there is no consideration for the transfer of assets, functions, and risks, or taxpayers reduce their operating profit by more than 20%.

The disclosure of a reportable scheme must include the following information:

General information about the taxpayer and advisors, and, where applicable, the legal representative; a detailed description of the scheme and its applicable national and international regulations; a description of the tax benefit obtained, as well as the fiscal years in which it was implemented.

Pursuant to Article 199 of the Federal Tax Code, any scheme that generates or may generate, directly or indirectly, a tax benefit in Mexico and has any of the following characteristics is considered a reportable scheme:

I. Prevents foreign authorities from exchanging tax or financial information with Mexican tax authorities, including through the application of the Standard for the Automatic Exchange of Information on Financial Accounts in Tax Matters, as referred to in the recommendation adopted by the OECD Council on July 15, 2014, as well as other similar forms of information exchange. In the case of the aforementioned Standard, this section will not apply to the extent that the taxpayer has received documentation from an intermediary demonstrating that the information has been disclosed by said intermediary to the relevant foreign tax authority. The provisions of this section include when an account, financial product, or investment that is not a financial account is used for the purposes of the aforementioned Standard, or when income or capital is reclassified into products not subject to information exchange.

II. Avoid the application of Article 4-B or Chapter I, Title VI, of the Income Tax Law.

III. Consists of one or more legal acts that allow the transfer of tax losses pending reduction from taxable profits to persons other than those who generated them.

IV. Consists of a series of interconnected payments or transactions that return all or part of the amount of the first payment that is part of said series to the person who made it or one of its partners, shareholders, or related parties.

V. Involves a foreign resident who applies a double taxation agreement signed by Mexico with respect to income that is not taxed in the taxpayer's country or jurisdiction of tax residence. The provisions of this section shall also apply when said income is taxed at a reduced rate compared to the corporate rate in the taxpayer's country or jurisdiction of tax residence.

VI. Involves transactions between related parties in which:

a) Intangible assets that are difficult to value are transferred in accordance with the Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations, approved by the OECD Council in 1995, or any subsequent guidelines. An intangible asset is considered difficult to value when, at the time the transaction is carried out, there are no reliable comparables, or the projections of future cash flows or income expected to be obtained from the intangible asset, or the assumptions for its valuation, are uncertain, making it difficult to predict the ultimate success of the intangible asset at the time it is transferred;

b) Corporate restructurings are carried out in which there is no consideration for the transfer of assets, functions, and risks, or when, as a result of such restructuring, taxpayers who pay taxes under Title II of the Income Tax Law reduce their operating profit by more than 20%. Corporate restructurings are those referred to in the Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations, approved by the OECD Council in 1995, or any subsequent guidelines;

c) The transfer or temporary use or enjoyment of assets and rights is granted without consideration, or services are provided or functions are performed that are not remunerated;

d) There are no reliable comparables, because the transactions involve unique or valuable functions or assets, or

e) A unilateral protection regime granted under foreign legislation is used in accordance with the Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations, approved by the OECD Council in 1995, or any subsequent regulations.

VII. Avoid establishing a permanent establishment in Mexico under the Income Tax Law and the double taxation treaties signed by Mexico.

VIII. Involves the transfer of a fully or partially depreciated asset, allowing its depreciation by another related party.

IX. When it involves a hybrid mechanism defined in accordance with Section XXIII of Article 28 of the Income Tax Law.

X. Avoid the identification of the beneficial owner of income or assets, including through the use of foreign entities or legal entities whose beneficiaries are not designated or identified at the time of their incorporation or at a later time.

XI. When there are tax losses whose deadline for reducing taxable income is about to expire pursuant to the Income Tax Law, and transactions are carried out to obtain taxable income, from which said tax losses are reduced, and said transactions generate an authorized deduction for the taxpayer who generated the losses or a related party.

XII. Avoid the application of the additional 10% rate provided for in Articles 140, second paragraph; 142, second paragraph of Section V; and 164 of the Income Tax Law.

XIII. In which the temporary use or enjoyment of an asset is granted, and the lessee in turn grants the temporary use or enjoyment of the same asset to the lessor or a related party of the latter.

XIV. Involves transactions whose accounting and tax records show differences greater than 20%, except for those arising from differences in the calculation of depreciation.

(b) Updates on marketable cross-border arrangements.

The provision clarifies that arrangements based on tax regimes expressly approved by the European Commission are excluded. Certain intermediaries may be exempt from reporting if bound by legal professional privilege, although they must notify the relevant taxpayer. The law also establishes a sanctioning regime: failure to report, late reporting, or providing incomplete/false information constitutes a serious tax infringement, punishable with fixed monetary penalties (generally €2,000 per item, with minimums of €4,000 and maximums linked to fees earned or tax benefits obtained).

Additional Provision 24th LGT introduces specific obligations of communication among intermediaries and taxpayers. For example, intermediaries who are exempt from reporting due to professional secrecy must inform their clients, and intermediaries or taxpayers who have filed a disclosure must notify the others involved, thereby relieving them of their reporting duty. Non-compliance with these communication duties is sanctioned with a fixed penalty of €600, which may increase if the lack of communication results in a failure to disclose the arrangement.

Article 49 ter RGAT provides regulatory detail on these obligations. It confirms that intermediaries and, in some cases, the relevant taxpayers, must report to the Spanish Tax Administration cross-border mechanisms involving CRS avoidance or opaque structures whenever the prescribed hallmarks are present. It defines when an arrangement is considered cross-border, identifies the criteria linking an intermediary to Spain (residence, permanent establishment, incorporation, or place of management), and sets the reporting deadline at thirty days from the triggering event. The regulation also specifies that reporting must cover all jurisdictions where the arrangement is made available, and that the hallmark related to CRS avoidance applies even if certain conditions are not strictly met.

In summary, Spain has a comprehensive mandatory disclosure regime that requires the reporting of cross-border tax planning arrangements, including CRS avoidance structures, with clearly defined obligations for intermediaries and taxpayers, as well as a specific penalty framework for non-compliance.
